Snyk.author: ButlerianJihad
Snyk.text: My father originally had a 100% manual lawnmower, and for the size of our property, it wasn't really bad; my father is a physically fit dude, and he could knock out the whole thing in a short period.Then in the late 80s, he purchased an electric lawnmower! Yep it wasn't battery-powered, but it had a little AC cord that you plugged in... somewhere! So Dad would just run a ginormous snake of an extension cord out across the lawn.Now, our property wasn't large, but to reach an AC outlet, we really needed a lot of cord, and of course it was a key skill to not run over your own cord, like when you're vacuuming.Dad never got anything gas-powered. He also had an edger that was electric, IIRC, and he made a lot of use of this edger. It was one of those kinds that used a fishing-line type cutting edge.But he kept that machine around, and I guess it was fine for a very long time. Dad and Mom are old enough to employ a landscaping team, nowadays.

SonarQube.author: onion2k
SonarQube.text: manual PR reviews can catch things that llms currently missI didn't say LLMs though. I'm talking about the sort of code quality tooling that's been in use for decades - Sonarqube, Codacy, CodeClimate, etc for code quality, eslint for AST-based code rule checking (easily picks up duplication for example), Istanbul for code coverage, Wiz or Github Advanced Security for security.These are well known industry standards for knowing a code change is correct without giving it to an LLM to guess at. If you have them, and they're well configured, and you maintain the tooling properly, then PRs become unhelpful gates that don't find problems.
